label: A Geometry You Can See
notes: The prologue, printed pages xvii through xxiii, sets the program for the whole book: differential geometry done with pictures and geometric reasoning instead of opaque symbol pushing. We open by stating the wager that curvature, transport, and forms can all be literally seen, and that this seeing is itself a kind of proof.

label: Against Opaque Calculation
notes: Needham contrasts two routes to the same identity: a blind chain of algebraic manipulations that yields a true formula no one understands, and a single diagram that makes the result obvious. We motivate the book's stance that a calculation which hides its geometric meaning has failed its main job, even when it is correct.

label: Newton's Ultimate Equality
notes: Here we introduce the core proof device: ultimate equality, written with the tilde. Two quantities are ultimately equal when their ratio tends to one as the construction shrinks. This is Newton's language for vanishing-to-higher-order, and it lets us replace curves by their tangents within any first-order computation without losing rigor.

label: Vanishing to Higher Order
notes: We make ultimate equality precise. Quantities agreeing to first order differ by terms of order epsilon squared, so dividing by the leading term sends the discrepancy to zero. We show that sums, products, and ratios of ultimately equal pieces stay ultimately equal, which is exactly what licenses substitution inside a shrinking diagram.

label: The Tangent Triangle
notes: We compute the derivative of tangent purely visually. A tiny angular increment produces an arc, a chord, and a thin triangle whose legs are ultimately equal to differentials. Reading the similar triangles off the picture gives the derivative directly, with no formula manipulation. This is the prologue's showcase of seeing replacing symbol shuffling.

label: Curvature Made Visible
notes: We preview the book's central promise: curvature is not an abstract tensor but something the eye can detect. A geodesic triangle on a sphere has angles summing to more than a straight angle, and that angular excess equals the enclosed curvature. We set up the picture students will return to throughout the metric and curvature acts.

label: Act I — The Nature of Space
notes: The first act asks what space itself is before any measurement is imposed. We sketch the move from flat Euclidean intuition to curved surfaces and to the idea that geometry is intrinsic, knowable by inhabitants who never leave their surface. This act supplies the stage on which the metric will later be installed.

label: Act II — The Metric
notes: The second act installs a ruler. A metric assigns lengths and angles to tangent vectors, so an infinitesimal patch carries an ellipse of measurement. We explain how the same surface admits many coordinate charts while the metric records what is genuinely geometric, distinguishing cosmetic relabeling from real distance.

label: Act III — Curvature
notes: The third act measures bending. We connect Gaussian curvature to angular excess and to the failure of parallel lines, and we foreshadow the global Gauss-Bonnet theorem linking total curvature to the Euler characteristic. The act turns the visible defect of a triangle into a precise, topology-aware invariant of the whole surface.

label: Act IV — Parallel Transport
notes: The fourth act moves vectors. Carrying a tangent vector around a closed loop while keeping it as parallel as the surface allows returns it rotated, and that holonomy angle measures the curvature enclosed by the loop. We frame transport as a physical probe, the operational way an inhabitant detects curvature without ever leaving home.

label: Act V — Forms
notes: The fifth act builds measurement machines. A differential form eats directed pieces of geometry and returns oriented numbers; a one-form reads stacks crossed, a two-form reads signed area swept. We motivate forms as the natural bookkeeping for orientation and flux, with the wedge product detecting sign and the exterior derivative unifying the classical theorems.

label: The Five-Act Argument
notes: We close by drawing the dependency map: space supports a metric, the metric reveals curvature, curvature is probed by transport, and forms package every measurement with orientation. The acts are one continuous argument, not six topics, and each rests on the single visual habit of letting a shrinking picture carry the proof. Pages xvii to xxiii.
